{"id":"SMA-621","uuid":"84824b54-31f4-4bcf-9c61-37eebdff0b23","title":"ModelTurnAccumulator merges parallel blank-call_id tool calls, failing the turn on concatenated args","description":"Raised by CodeRabbit on the <issue id="c590d5a2-5978-4bed-bfda-915404efc5d2" label="SMA-619" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-619/litellm-upgrades-a-blank-call-id-after-emission-splitting-one-call" /> PR (#249, thread [r3948857802](<https://github.com/SMK1085/paigasus-helikon/pull/249#discussion_r3948857802>)) and deferred there as out of scope. <issue id="c590d5a2-5978-4bed-bfda-915404efc5d2" label="SMA-619" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-619/litellm-upgrades-a-blank-call-id-after-emission-splitting-one-call" /> pinned the cost with a test rather than fixing it; this is the ticket that owns the fix, if we want one.

## The defect

`ModelTurnAccumulator::observe` groups tool-call deltas by `call_id` (`crates/paigasus-helikon-core/src/model.rs:594`) with no exemption for the blank id, joins each group's `args_delta`s into one string, and parses that string exactly once (`model.rs:539-544`). A parse failure propagates out of `finish()` (`model.rs:624`) and discards the **entire turn, assistant text included**.

So N parallel tool calls that all arrive under `call_id: ""` collapse into a single `Item::ToolCall`, first-name-wins, with every call's arguments concatenated:

```text
("", Some("alpha"), "")  ("", Some("beta"), "")
("", None, "{\"p\":1}")  ("", None, "{\"q\":2}")

-> one item, name "alpha", args_str "{\"p\":1}{\"q\":2}" -> Err, whole turn dropped
```

`beta` is lost outright. With no arguments at all the turn survives but still yields one call where the backend sent two.

## This is documented, not accidental

`ModelEvent::ToolCallDelta`'s contract (`model.rs:189-197`, tightened by <issue id="d345d77f-6510-4c89-9aad-3bb196bfcedc" label="SMA-616" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-616/litellm-flush-buffered-names-drops-a-blank-id-calls-name-via-the-call" />) states the rule and then states that this crate breaks it:

> The non-blank qualifier is deliberate. A backend may send `"id": ""`, and an empty id cannot identify a call — so a provider MUST NOT merge two parallel blank-id calls, and two such calls therefore each carry a name under `""`. Consumers that need one entry per call should key on a non-blank `call_id` and treat `""` as "unidentified". This crate's own `ModelTurnAccumulator` does not follow that advice: it deliberately merges blank-id calls together, first-name-wins, the same as any other `call_id`.

The translators hold up their end — `providers-litellm` and `openai/chat` both emit one name-carrying delta per blank-id call, pinned by `blank_ids_do_not_collapse_distinct_calls` and `blank_ids_do_not_collapse_at_end_of_stream` in each. The gap is entirely between the event layer and the accumulator.

## Why it is more reachable after <issue id="c590d5a2-5978-4bed-bfda-915404efc5d2" label="SMA-619" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-619/litellm-upgrades-a-blank-call-id-after-emission-splitting-one-call" />

<issue id="c590d5a2-5978-4bed-bfda-915404efc5d2" label="SMA-619" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-619/litellm-upgrades-a-blank-call-id-after-emission-splitting-one-call" /> stops a blank `call_id` being upgraded to a real one once a delta has already gone out under `""` — otherwise one call splits across two ids and the real one carries no name. Keeping the call under `""` is the right call at the event layer, but it means streams that previously ended up under real ids now stay blank, so **more** streams reach the accumulator merge. <issue id="c590d5a2-5978-4bed-bfda-915404efc5d2" label="SMA-619" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-619/litellm-upgrades-a-blank-call-id-after-emission-splitting-one-call" /> did not change the accumulator; it widened the input set.

Pinned there by `withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged` (`crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-litellm/src/stream.rs`), which asserts `finish()` returns `Err` and records the trade as accepted. That test is the thing to update if this is fixed.

## Nothing downstream defends against it

There is no validation of a blank `call_id` anywhere in the loop. `build_items` constructs `Item::ToolCall { call_id: "", .. }` unconditionally and defaults a missing name to `""` (`model.rs:545-549`); `loop_state.rs:278-300` dispatches on the presence of an `Item::ToolCall` and matches handoffs by `name` with no check that the call is identifiable. A blank-id call that *does* survive is dispatched as a tool named `""`.

## Options

1. **Exempt the blank id in the accumulator** — give each blank-id delta run its own bucket rather than keying on `""`. Cheapest, and confined to `core`. Needs a rule for what separates two runs, since the only signal is delta ordering.
2. **Surface it as an error** — refuse to build an `Item::ToolCall` with a blank `call_id` and return a `ModelError`/violation instead. Honest, but changes the `ModelEvent` contract and needs every translator moved in lockstep. This is <issue id="c590d5a2-5978-4bed-bfda-915404efc5d2" label="SMA-619" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-619/litellm-upgrades-a-blank-call-id-after-emission-splitting-one-call" /> spec §2.3's considered-and-rejected alternative, rejected on scope rather than on merit.
3. **Do nothing, document harder.** The current state: accurate docs, a test pinning the cost, and a `warn!` naming each discarded id.

## Scope warning

Whatever is chosen, this is a **cross-provider** change, not a `core`-only one. Six translators carry blank-id handling (`providers-litellm`, `openai/chat`, `openai/responses`, `providers-anthropic`, `providers-bedrock`, `providers-gemini`), and `openai/responses` has no blank-id handling at all — its own name-dedup defect is open as <issue id="3babda5a-6506-488b-aefb-c4dfe16aab1e" label="SMA-617" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-617/openairesponses-can-emit-two-name-carrying-deltas-for-one-call-id-via" />. `tests/provider-stream-conformance`'s assertion 7 (`src/check.rs`) is deliberately **not** scoped to non-blank ids, and its comment says the first blank-id fixture to arrive will trip it — that is the decision point this ticket would reach.

## Acceptance criteria

* A decision is recorded between options 1-3, with the reasoning, before any code changes.
* If 1 or 2: two parallel blank-id calls carrying distinct arguments survive `ModelTurnAccumulator::finish()` as two items, or fail with a diagnostic that names the ambiguity — not with a `serde_json` trailing-characters error.
* A test drives that shape and is verified to FAIL against `main` first.
* `withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged` and `ModelEvent::ToolCallDelta`'s doc comment are updated to match whatever is decided; neither may be left asserting the old behaviour.
* The conformance suite's assertion 7 is either left unscoped deliberately or scoped with the reasoning recorded in `check.rs`.","priority":{"value":4,"name":"Low"},"url":"https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-621/modelturnaccumulator-merges-parallel-blank-call-id-tool-calls-failing","gitBranchName":"feature/sma-621-modelturnaccumulator-merges-parallel-blank","createdAt":"2026-09-07T17:56:48.500Z","updatedAt":"2026-11-21T10:01:49.267Z","archivedAt":null,"completedAt":null,"startedAt":"2026-11-21T10:01:49.250Z","canceledAt":null,"dueDate":null,"slaStartedAt":null,"slaMediumRiskAt":null,"slaHighRiskAt":null,"slaBreachesAt":null,"status":"In Progress","statusType":"started","labels":["area:providers","area:core","stage:3","Bug"],"attachments":[],"documents":[],"createdBy":"Sven Maschek","createdById":"ba6021cb-56c5-43aa-9797-fab3599d7ead","assignee":"Sven Maschek","assigneeId":"ba6021cb-56c5-43aa-9797-fab3599d7ead","project":"Paigasus Helikon","projectId":"5d1fd72d-af2d-40f5-b562-fa04f8018610","team":"Sven Maschek","teamId":"7178572e-d61f-4cf0-bbcb-4e03c8d9f39e"}

Base directory for this skill: /Users/smaschek/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.2/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

I read the accumulator, the litellm tests, and conformance assertion 7. Here is what I found.

**What you want.** You want two parallel tool calls with `call_id: ""` to stop failing the full turn with a `serde_json` "trailing characters" error. The ticket needs a recorded decision first, then a fix and test updates.

**The important finding: option 1 cannot be done safely.** Option 1 separates the blank-id calls by delta order. But the translators send the deltas interleaved, not one call after the other. The existing test `withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged` shows this order:

```text
("", "alpha", "")   ("", "beta", "")   ("", None, {"p":1})   ("", None, {"q":2})
```

The `index` that identified each call is gone at the event layer. So a "new name starts a new bucket" rule gives all the arguments to `beta`. That is worse than the current failure. If `beta` has no arguments, `alpha`'s arguments go to `beta`, the JSON parses, and the wrong tool runs with the wrong arguments. Nothing reports this.

**Approaches:**

- **A. Fail loudly in `core` (my pick).** If a second name arrives under `""`, `finish()` returns an error like "2 parallel tool calls with a blank call_id; arguments cannot be attributed". The change stays in `core`. There is no contract break and no translator change. Cost: the turn still fails. Also, the zero-argument case that today gives `Ok` with one call (and loses `beta`) now fails too.
- **B. Translators make distinct ids** from `index` for blank-id calls. This gives two real items. But it reverses SMA-619's "keep it under `""`" decision, sends ids the backend never issued, and touches six translators.
- **C. Do nothing (option 3).** This does not satisfy the acceptance criteria.

I recommend A. It is the only approach that never guesses. Which approach do you want?

# SMA-621: refuse parallel blank-`call_id` tool calls in `ModelTurnAccumulator`

Status: draft for approval. Size: small change, confined to `core` plus doc and test
updates in two provider crates and the conformance suite.

## Intent

`ModelTurnAccumulator::observe` groups `ToolCallDelta`s by `call_id`. It does not
exempt the blank id `""`. So N parallel calls that arrive under `""` become one
`Item::ToolCall`. The first name wins and the arguments of all calls concatenate.

- With arguments, the concatenation (`{"p":1}{"q":2}`) fails to parse. `finish()`
  returns a `serde_json` "trailing characters" error and the run fails with no
  explanation of the real cause.
- With no arguments, `finish()` returns `Ok` with one call. The second call is lost
  and nothing reports it.

The goal: the accumulator must never guess, and a failure must name the real cause.

## Decision (acceptance criterion 1)

The ticket offers three options. Sven picked a core-only form of option 2 on
2026-11-21 ("Approach A").

| Approach | What it does | Why it was not picked / was picked |
|----------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| 1. Separate blank-id runs by delta order | A new name under `""` starts a new bucket. Nameless deltas go to the latest bucket. | **Rejected.** The translators emit blank-id deltas interleaved (`withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged` emits name, name, args, args). The `index` that told the calls apart does not exist at the event layer. Order-based buckets give every argument to the last call. If that call has no arguments of its own, the JSON parses and the **wrong tool runs with another call's arguments**, with no error. A silent misattribution is worse than the current loud failure. |
| B. Translators make distinct ids from `index` | `providers-litellm` and `openai/chat` replace `""` with a synthetic id. | **Rejected.** It reverses the SMA-619 decision to keep such a call under `""`, it sends the backend ids that the backend never issued, and it touches six translators. |
| **A. Refuse in the accumulator (picked)** | If more than one name-carrying delta arrives under `""`, `finish()` returns an error that names the ambiguity. | **Picked.** It is the only approach that never guesses. It changes no public signature and no translator. |
| 3. Do nothing | Keep the docs and the pinning test. | **Rejected.** It does not satisfy acceptance criterion 2. |

Approach A is option 2 confined to `core`. The ticket's option 2 refuses **every**
blank-id call and needs every translator to change. Approach A refuses only the
ambiguous case (two or more calls under `""`). A single blank-id call keeps its
current behaviour.

## Design

### Detection

- `ModelTurnAccumulator` counts the name-carrying (`name: Some(_)`) deltas it
  observes under `call_id == ""`, and keeps those names in arrival order.
- A count of 2 or more means two or more calls. The `ToolCallDelta` contract says
  each blank-id call carries its own name under `""`. Two equal names (`"alpha"`,
  `"alpha"`) are two calls, so the count does not de-duplicate names.
- A count of 0 or 1 keeps the current behaviour exactly: the deltas merge into one
  bucket and the item has `call_id: ""`.
- Non-blank ids keep the current behaviour exactly, including first-name-wins.
  This change does not touch them.

### Failure

- `finish()` checks for the ambiguous case **before** it parses any arguments. So
  the ambiguity error replaces the `serde_json` error, and the zero-argument case
  fails too.
- The return type stays `Result<ModelTurn, String>`. No public signature changes.
- The message names the cause, the count and the names. Proposed text:
  `ambiguous tool calls: 2 parallel tool calls arrived under a blank call_id (names: "alpha", "beta"); their arguments cannot be attributed to a call`.
- Callers need no change. `agent.rs` turns the `Err` into `AgentError::Other` and
  `AgentEvent::RunFailed { error }`. `runtime-temporal` turns it into
  `ErrorKindPayload::Other`. Both pass the text through.
- The full turn still fails, assistant text included. That is the same outcome as
  today's argument case. Keeping the text and dropping only the calls would hand the
  loop a turn that silently lost its tool calls, which is the class of defect this
  change removes.

### Behaviour change

The zero-argument case changes from `Ok` (one call, one lost) to `Err`. This is
deliberate: today `beta` disappears with no signal. The change is a `fix` with no
signature change, so release-plz gives `core` a patch bump. No hand-bumped version.

## Updates the ticket requires

1. **New `core` tests** in `model.rs` `model_turn_tests`. Each test must FAIL on
   `main` first (acceptance criterion 3):
   - two blank-id calls with distinct arguments: `finish()` is `Err`, and the
     message contains `blank call_id` and both names (on `main` it is a `serde_json`
     error, so the message assertion fails);
   - two blank-id calls with no arguments: `finish()` is `Err` (on `main` it is `Ok`);
   - control cases that must pass on `main` and after the change: one blank-id call
     gives one `Ok` item with `call_id: ""`; two non-blank calls give two items.
2. **`ModelEvent::ToolCallDelta` doc comment** (`model.rs:190-197`): replace "does
   not follow that advice: it deliberately merges blank-id calls" with the new rule.
   One blank-id call is accumulated; two or more make `finish()` fail.
3. **`ModelTurn` / `finish()` docs**: state the new error case.
4. **`withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged`**
   (`providers-litellm/src/stream.rs`): rename it (proposed:
   `withheld_upgrades_make_parallel_blank_calls_fail_loudly`). Assert that the error
   text names the ambiguity, not only `is_err()`. Rewrite its doc comment and the
   other stale references in that file (around lines 2228 and 2357-2365).
5. **`openai/chat.rs:692`** and **`openai/responses.rs:409, 1166`**: update any
   comment that describes the old merge.
6. **Conformance assertion 7** (`tests/provider-stream-conformance/src/check.rs`):
   leave it **unscoped, deliberately**, and rewrite the comment with the reason.
   Assertion 7 is an event-layer check. Two names under `""` are legal at the event
   layer, but after this change `ModelTurnAccumulator` refuses that turn. So a
   fixture that shows two blank-id names is a stream that fails in production. A
   red gate on that fixture is the correct signal. A future blank-id fixture with
   one call passes assertion 7 as it is now.

## Non-goals

- No change to any translator's event output.
- No validation of a single blank-id call. It still dispatches with `call_id: ""`.
  Whether a backend accepts `""` on replay is a separate question and out of scope.
- No change for non-blank ids, including the SMA-617 name-dedup defect in
  `openai/responses`.
- No change to the `ModelEvent` contract beyond the documentation of the
  accumulator's own behaviour.

## Anti-goals

- The change must never produce a turn in which a tool runs with another call's
  arguments.
- The change must never turn the current loud failure into a silent loss.

## Left to the builder

- The exact wording of the error message, if it contains `blank call_id`, the count
  and the names.
- Whether the count lives in a field on `ModelTurnAccumulator` or on the `""`
  `ToolCallAccum`.
- Whether the mdBook or the `core` README mention the merge behaviour. If they do,
  update them in the same PR. If not, record that no book or README edit is needed.

- A count of 2 or more means two or more calls. The `ToolCallDelta` contract says
  each blank-id call carries its own name under `""`. Two equal names (`"alpha"`,
  `"alpha"`) are two calls, so the count does not de-duplicate names.
- A count of 0 or 1 keeps the current behaviour exactly: the deltas merge into one
  bucket and the item has `call_id: ""`.
- Non-blank ids keep the current behaviour exactly, including first-name-wins.
  This change does not touch them.

### Failure

- `finish()` checks for the ambiguous case **before** it parses any arguments. So
  the ambiguity error replaces the `serde_json` error, and the zero-argument case
  fails too.
- The return type stays `Result<ModelTurn, String>`. No public signature changes.
- The message names the cause, the count and the names. Proposed text:
  `ambiguous tool calls: 2 parallel tool calls arrived under a blank call_id (names: "alpha", "beta"); their arguments cannot be attributed to a call`.
- Callers need no change. `agent.rs` turns the `Err` into `AgentError::Other` and
  `AgentEvent::RunFailed { error }`. `runtime-temporal` turns it into
  `ErrorKindPayload::Other`. Both pass the text through.
- The full turn still fails, assistant text included. That is the same outcome as
  today's argument case. Keeping the text and dropping only the calls would hand the
  loop a turn that silently lost its tool calls, which is the class of defect this
  change removes.

### Behaviour change

The zero-argument case changes from `Ok` (one call, one lost) to `Err`. This is
deliberate: today `beta` disappears with no signal. The change is a `fix` with no
signature change, so release-plz gives `core` a patch bump. No hand-bumped version.

## Updates the ticket requires

1. **New `core` tests** in `model.rs` `model_turn_tests`. Each test must FAIL on
   `main` first (acceptance criterion 3):
   - two blank-id calls with distinct arguments: `finish()` is `Err`, and the
     message contains `blank call_id` and both names (on `main` it is a `serde_json`
     error, so the message assertion fails);
   - two blank-id calls with no arguments: `finish()` is `Err` (on `main` it is `Ok`);
   - control cases that must pass on `main` and after the change: one blank-id call
     gives one `Ok` item with `call_id: ""`; two non-blank calls give two items.
2. **`ModelEvent::ToolCallDelta` doc comment** (`model.rs:190-197`): replace "does
   not follow that advice: it deliberately merges blank-id calls" with the new rule.
   One blank-id call is accumulated; two or more make `finish()` fail.
3. **`ModelTurn` / `finish()` docs**: state the new error case.
4. **`withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged`**
   (`providers-litellm/src/stream.rs`): rename it (proposed:
   `withheld_upgrades_make_parallel_blank_calls_fail_loudly`). Assert that the error
   text names the ambiguity, not only `is_err()`. Rewrite its doc comment and the
   other stale references in that file (around lines 2228 and 2357-2365).
5. **`openai/chat.rs:692`** and **`openai/responses.rs:409, 1166`**: update any
   comment that describes the old merge.
6. **Conformance assertion 7** (`tests/provider-stream-conformance/src/check.rs`):
   leave it **unscoped, deliberately**, and rewrite the comment with the reason.
   Assertion 7 is an event-layer check. Two names under `""` are legal at the event
   layer, but after this change `ModelTurnAccumulator` refuses that turn. So a
   fixture that shows two blank-id names is a stream that fails in production. A
   red gate on that fixture is the correct signal. A future blank-id fixture with
   one call passes assertion 7 as it is now.

## Non-goals

- No change to any translator's event output.
- No validation of a single blank-id call. It still dispatches with `call_id: ""`.
  Whether a backend accepts `""` on replay is a separate question and out of scope.
- No change for non-blank ids, including the SMA-617 name-dedup defect in
  `openai/responses`.
- No change to the `ModelEvent` contract beyond the documentation of the
  accumulator's own behaviour.

## Anti-goals

- The change must never produce a turn in which a tool runs with another call's
  arguments.
- The change must never turn the current loud failure into a silent loss.

## Left to the builder

- The exact wording of the error message, if it contains `blank call_id`, the count
  and the names.
- Whether the count lives in a field on `ModelTurnAccumulator` or on the `""`
  `ToolCallAccum`.
- Whether the mdBook or the `core` README mention the merge behaviour. If they do,
  update them in the same PR. If not, record that no book or README edit is needed.

    - openai/chat: once per index (`chat.rs:842-849`)
    - openai/responses: once per item (`responses.rs:362-365, 592`)
    - anthropic and bedrock: once per block (`anthropic stream.rs:135-140`, `bedrock stream.rs:171-176`)
    - gemini: one named delta per part (`gemini stream.rs:47-51`)
  
    The AG-UI mapper also assumes this invariant (`agui/map.rs:45-46, 62`). Two residual shapes remain:
    - False positive: a malformed backend moves one blank-id call across two wire keys (chat: two `index` values, which are not aliased because `canonicalize` returns early for `""` at `chat.rs:552-561`; litellm: `Index` to positional).     | Why it matters: Anti-goal 1 is absolute, but the design meets it only for streams that obey the contract. | Suggested fix: write "exactly one name-carrying delta per blank-id call" into the `ToolCallDelta` doc.     - equal names (`alpha`, `alpha`) give `Err` (a mutant that de-duplicates names passes every planned test);

  - Which real backends send `"id": ""`? The SMA-616 spec (line 260) says the repo has no blank-id capture. If no backend is known, say so, because that limits the effect of the zero-argument change from `Ok` to `Err`.   - No current test depends on the merge returning `Ok`. The litellm `accumulated()` calls at `stream.rs:2206, 2275, 2346` use one blank-id call, so their results do not change. The call at `2425` already expects `Err` and changes only the reason. No test in `core`, `providers-openai` or the conformance suite drives two names under `""` through the accumulator.

# SMA-621: refuse parallel blank-`call_id` tool calls in `ModelTurnAccumulator`

Status: draft for approval (revised after the adversarial spec challenge).
Size: small change. The behaviour change is in `core`. The other edits are docs and
tests in `providers-litellm`, `runtime-temporal` and the conformance suite.

## Intent

`ModelTurnAccumulator::observe` groups `ToolCallDelta`s by `call_id`
(`core/src/model.rs:594-600`). It does not exempt the blank id `""`. So N parallel
calls that arrive under `""` become one `Item::ToolCall`. The first name wins and the
arguments of all calls concatenate. On `main` this has three outcomes:

1. **Loud, wrong cause.** Two calls carry arguments. The concatenation
   (`{"p":1}{"q":2}`) fails to parse. `finish()` returns a `serde_json` "trailing
   characters" error, and the run fails with no statement of the real cause.
2. **Silent loss.** Two calls carry no arguments. `finish()` returns `Ok` with one
   call. The second call is lost and nothing reports it.
3. **Silent misattribution.** The first call carries no arguments and the second
   call does: `("", Some("delete_all"), "")`, then `("", Some("search"), "{\"q\":1}")`.
   The joined text parses. `finish()` returns `Ok`, and **`delete_all` runs with
   `search`'s arguments**. Both chat translators can emit this shape: a delta with no
   name fragment flushes the name with empty arguments (`openai/chat.rs:842-849`,
   `providers-litellm/src/stream.rs:580-587`).

The goal: the accumulator must never guess, and a failure must name the real cause.

No blank-id capture exists in the repo (SMA-616 spec), and no known backend is
recorded as one that sends `"id": ""`. So the effect of outcomes 2 and 3 changing
from `Ok` to `Err` on real users is not known. `ModelSettings` has no
`parallel_tool_calls` setting (`model.rs:137-157`), so a user who hits the new error
has no workaround in this crate.

## Decision (acceptance criterion 1)

The ticket offers options 1, 2 and 3. Sven picked "Approach A" on 2026-11-21. It is a
`core`-only form of ticket option 2.

| Row | Ticket option | What it does | Result and reason |
|-----|---------------|--------------|-------------------|
| A | 2, limited to `core` | If two or more name-carrying deltas arrive under `""`, `finish()` returns an error that names the ambiguity. | **Picked.** It is the only approach that never guesses. It changes no public signature and no translator. Its signal ("a second name is a new call") is the rule that `agui/map.rs:45-46, 62` already uses, so `core` and the AG-UI mapper agree on what a call is. |
| Order buckets | 1 | A new name under `""` starts a new bucket. Nameless deltas go to the latest bucket. | **Rejected.** The translators emit blank-id deltas interleaved: `withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged` emits name, name, args, args. The `index` that told the calls apart does not exist at the event layer. Order buckets give every argument to the last call. If that call has no arguments of its own, the JSON parses and the wrong tool runs with another call's arguments. |
| Split self-contained deltas | 1, a narrow form | If two or more names arrive under `""` and no nameless delta carries arguments, make one item per name. | **Rejected.** It does not guess, but it makes two or more items with the same `call_id: ""`. Downstream code matches on `call_id`: `loop_state.rs:445` (`deferred.iter().any(\|p\| p.call_id() == c.call_id)`) marks both calls pending when only one is deferred, `resume_exec.rs:176` resolves to the first match, and the provider request translators pair each tool result to its call by id. Two items with one id break all three. |
| Synthetic ids | not in the ticket | `providers-litellm` and `openai/chat` replace `""` with an id made from `index`. | **Rejected.** It reverses the SMA-619 decision to keep such a call under `""`. (Gemini already makes `fc_{n}` ids when the backend sends none, so a synthetic id is not new to the repo. The SMA-619 reason alone is enough.) |
| Do nothing | 3 | Keep the docs and the pinning test. | **Rejected.** It does not satisfy acceptance criterion 2, and it keeps outcome 3. |

Ticket option 2 refuses **every** blank-id call and needs every translator to change.
Approach A refuses only the ambiguous case. A single blank-id call keeps its current
behaviour.

## Design

### Contract

The `ModelEvent::ToolCallDelta` doc comment (`model.rs:183-197`) now states the
invariant that the detection needs: **each blank-id call carries exactly one
name-carrying delta**. It says today only that two such calls "each carry a name".
All six translators already comply. The challenge checked each one: litellm once per
key, openai/chat once per index, openai/responses once per item, anthropic and
bedrock once per block, gemini once per part. This is a doc change to the contract
that records the current behaviour. It does not change what any translator emits.

### Detection

- `ModelTurnAccumulator` counts the deltas with `name: Some(_)` that it observes
  under `call_id == ""`, and keeps those names in arrival order.
- `Some("")` counts. It is a name-carrying delta. No translator emits it today.
- Equal names count separately. `"alpha"`, `"alpha"` are two calls under the
  contract, so the count does not de-duplicate.
- A count of 0 or 1 keeps the current behaviour exactly: the deltas merge into one
  bucket and the item has `call_id: ""`.
- Non-blank ids keep the current behaviour exactly, including first-name-wins.

### Failure

- `finish()` checks for the ambiguous case **before** it parses any arguments, for
  every bucket. So the ambiguity error replaces any `serde_json` error in the same
  turn, and outcomes 2 and 3 fail too.
- The whole turn fails, also when a valid non-blank call is in the same turn and
  assistant text is present. That is the same outcome as today's outcome 1. Keeping
  the text and dropping the calls would hand the loop a turn that silently lost its
  tool calls, which is the class of defect this change removes.
- The return type stays `Result<ModelTurn, String>`. No public signature changes.
- The message starts with the stable prefix `ambiguous tool calls:`. Then it gives the
  count and the names. Proposed text:
  `ambiguous tool calls: 2 parallel tool calls arrived under a blank call_id (names: "alpha", "beta"); their arguments cannot be attributed to a call`.
- Message constraints. Tool names come from the model, and the message reaches
  clients through `AgentEvent::RunFailed` (`agent.rs:1514`) and AG-UI.
  - Format each name with `{:?}`, so control characters are escaped.
  - List at most 8 names, then write `and N more`. Cut each name at 64 characters.
  - Never put argument text in the message. Arguments can contain secrets.
- `finish()` also writes a `tracing::warn!` with the count and the names (same
  constraints). The reason: `agent.rs:1511-1512` records only
  `otel.status_code = ERROR` on the span, not the message. `core` already depends
  on `tracing`.
- Callers need no change. `agent.rs:1508-1516` turns the `Err` into
  `AgentError::Other` and `RunFailed { error }`. `runtime-temporal`
  (`activities.rs:97-111`) turns it into `ErrorKindPayload::Other`, which is a

   call. The second call is lost and nothing reports it.

   `search`'s arguments**. Both chat translators can emit this shape: a delta with no
   name fragment flushes the name with empty arguments (`openai/chat.rs:842-849`,

# SMA-621: refuse parallel blank-`call_id` tool calls in `ModelTurnAccumulator`

Status: draft for approval. Size: small change, confined to `core` plus doc and test
updates in two provider crates and the conformance suite.

## Intent

`ModelTurnAccumulator::observe` groups `ToolCallDelta`s by `call_id`. It does not
exempt the blank id `""`. So N parallel calls that arrive under `""` become one
`Item::ToolCall`. The first name wins and the arguments of all calls concatenate.

- With arguments, the concatenation (`{"p":1}{"q":2}`) fails to parse. `finish()`
  returns a `serde_json` "trailing characters" error and the run fails with no
  explanation of the real cause.
- With no arguments, `finish()` returns `Ok` with one call. The second call is lost
  and nothing reports it.

The goal: the accumulator must never guess, and a failure must name the real cause.

## Decision (acceptance criterion 1)

The ticket offers three options. Sven picked a core-only form of option 2 on
2026-11-21 ("Approach A").

| Approach | What it does | Why it was not picked / was picked |
|----------|--------------|------------------------------------|
| 1. Separate blank-id runs by delta order | A new name under `""` starts a new bucket. Nameless deltas go to the latest bucket. | **Rejected.** The translators emit blank-id deltas interleaved (`withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged` emits name, name, args, args). The `index` that told the calls apart does not exist at the event layer. Order-based buckets give every argument to the last call. If that call has no arguments of its own, the JSON parses and the **wrong tool runs with another call's arguments**, with no error. A silent misattribution is worse than the current loud failure. |
| B. Translators make distinct ids from `index` | `providers-litellm` and `openai/chat` replace `""` with a synthetic id. | **Rejected.** It reverses the SMA-619 decision to keep such a call under `""`, it sends the backend ids that the backend never issued, and it touches six translators. |
| **A. Refuse in the accumulator (picked)** | If more than one name-carrying delta arrives under `""`, `finish()` returns an error that names the ambiguity. | **Picked.** It is the only approach that never guesses. It changes no public signature and no translator. |
| 3. Do nothing | Keep the docs and the pinning test. | **Rejected.** It does not satisfy acceptance criterion 2. |

Approach A is option 2 confined to `core`. The ticket's option 2 refuses **every**
blank-id call and needs every translator to change. Approach A refuses only the
ambiguous case (two or more calls under `""`). A single blank-id call keeps its
current behaviour.

## Design

### Detection

- `ModelTurnAccumulator` counts the name-carrying (`name: Some(_)`) deltas it
  observes under `call_id == ""`, and keeps those names in arrival order.
- A count of 2 or more means two or more calls. The `ToolCallDelta` contract says
  each blank-id call carries its own name under `""`. Two equal names (`"alpha"`,
  `"alpha"`) are two calls, so the count does not de-duplicate names.
- A count of 0 or 1 keeps the current behaviour exactly: the deltas merge into one
  bucket and the item has `call_id: ""`.
- Non-blank ids keep the current behaviour exactly, including first-name-wins.
  This change does not touch them.

### Failure

- `finish()` checks for the ambiguous case **before** it parses any arguments. So
  the ambiguity error replaces the `serde_json` error, and the zero-argument case
  fails too.
- The return type stays `Result<ModelTurn, String>`. No public signature changes.
- The message names the cause, the count and the names. Proposed text:
  `ambiguous tool calls: 2 parallel tool calls arrived under a blank call_id (names: "alpha", "beta"); their arguments cannot be attributed to a call`.
- Callers need no change. `agent.rs` turns the `Err` into `AgentError::Other` and
  `AgentEvent::RunFailed { error }`. `runtime-temporal` turns it into
  `ErrorKindPayload::Other`. Both pass the text through.
- The full turn still fails, assistant text included. That is the same outcome as
  today's argument case. Keeping the text and dropping only the calls would hand the
  loop a turn that silently lost its tool calls, which is the class of defect this
  change removes.

### Behaviour change

The zero-argument case changes from `Ok` (one call, one lost) to `Err`. This is
deliberate: today `beta` disappears with no signal. The change is a `fix` with no
signature change, so release-plz gives `core` a patch bump. No hand-bumped version.

## Updates the ticket requires

1. **New `core` tests** in `model.rs` `model_turn_tests`. Each test must FAIL on
   `main` first (acceptance criterion 3):
   - two blank-id calls with distinct arguments: `finish()` is `Err`, and the
     message contains `blank call_id` and both names (on `main` it is a `serde_json`
     error, so the message assertion fails);
   - two blank-id calls with no arguments: `finish()` is `Err` (on `main` it is `Ok`);
   - control cases that must pass on `main` and after the change: one blank-id call
     gives one `Ok` item with `call_id: ""`; two non-blank calls give two items.
2. **`ModelEvent::ToolCallDelta` doc comment** (`model.rs:190-197`): replace "does
   not follow that advice: it deliberately merges blank-id calls" with the new rule.
   One blank-id call is accumulated; two or more make `finish()` fail.
3. **`ModelTurn` / `finish()` docs**: state the new error case.
4. **`withheld_upgrades_keep_parallel_blank_calls_merged`**
   (`providers-litellm/src/stream.rs`): rename it (proposed:
   `withheld_upgrades_make_parallel_blank_calls_fail_loudly`). Assert that the error
   text names the ambiguity, not only `is_err()`. Rewrite its doc comment and the
   other stale references in that file (around lines 2228 and 2357-2365).
5. **`openai/chat.rs:692`** and **`openai/responses.rs:409, 1166`**: update any
   comment that describes the old merge.
6. **Conformance assertion 7** (`tests/provider-stream-conformance/src/check.rs`):
   leave it **unscoped, deliberately**, and rewrite the comment with the reason.
   Assertion 7 is an event-layer check. Two names under `""` are legal at the event
   layer, but after this change `ModelTurnAccumulator` refuses that turn. So a
   fixture that shows two blank-id names is a stream that fails in production. A
   red gate on that fixture is the correct signal. A future blank-id fixture with
   one call passes assertion 7 as it is now.

## Non-goals

- No change to any translator's event output.
- No validation of a single blank-id call. It still dispatches with `call_id: ""`.
  Whether a backend accepts `""` on replay is a separate question and out of scope.
- No change for non-blank ids, including the SMA-617 name-dedup defect in
  `openai/responses`.
- No change to the `ModelEvent` contract beyond the documentation of the
  accumulator's own behaviour.

## Anti-goals

- The change must never produce a turn in which a tool runs with another call's
  arguments.
- The change must never turn the current loud failure into a silent loss.

## Left to the builder

- The exact wording of the error message, if it contains `blank call_id`, the count
  and the names.
- Whether the count lives in a field on `ModelTurnAccumulator` or on the `""`
  `ToolCallAccum`.
- Whether the mdBook or the `core` README mention the merge behaviour. If they do,
  update them in the same PR. If not, record that no book or README edit is needed.

## Gate 1: spec approval

The revised spec is at `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-21-blank-call-id-accumulator-design.md` (in the worktree `.claude/worktrees/sma-621`).

**Challenger verdict:** approve with changes. There were no blockers, 4 major findings, and 9 minor findings. It agreed that Approach A is correct and found no reason to change the mechanism.

**What I changed:**

- **A third, worse defect on `main`.** I verified the challenger's main finding in `chat.rs:842-849`. If the first blank-id call has no arguments and the second call has arguments, `finish()` returns `Ok`. Then the first tool runs with the second tool's arguments, and nothing reports it. Approach A blocks this. A new test pins it.
- **Contract.** The `ToolCallDelta` doc now states "each blank-id call carries exactly one name-carrying delta". All six translators already work this way. The spec records two malformed-backend shapes as accepted limits: one false positive and one false negative.
- **Decision record.** I added a rejected row for "split into one item per name". It would make several items with the same `call_id: ""`, and `loop_state.rs:445`, `resume_exec.rs:176` and the request translators all match on `call_id`.
- **Assertion 7.** The old reasoning was contradictory. It would have blamed a correct translator. Now "exactly one name" applies only to non-blank ids, and `""` must have at least one name. This is my call, so correct it if you prefer to leave the gate unscoped.
- **Error message.** It starts with the stable prefix `ambiguous tool calls:`, escapes names with `{:?}`, lists at most 8 names, and never includes argument text. It also writes a `tracing::warn!`.

Do you approve the spec? You can also ask for changes, or for a second challenge run (`/challenge-spec`).

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter

  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

```

Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice

algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.
